teaching.causalExplanation: Pythagoras only works in a right-angled triangle, one with a square corner. So step one is always to find the right angle. It's marked with a little square. The side across from that corner has a special name, the hypotenuse. The hypotenuse is the longest side, opposite the right angle. Watch this triangle turn and flip. Wherever it ends up, the hypotenuse is still the side across from the little square. In the diamond, the right angle is at first base, so the hypotenuse is the throw from home to second. The other two sides, the ones that make the right angle, are the base paths. They're sometimes just called the shorter sides. Here's the idea behind the theorem. Take the garden bed triangle from before, with sides of three, four and five metres. Draw a square on each side. The square on the three side holds nine unit squares. The square on the four side holds sixteen. Now slide all of those into the big square on the hypotenuse. Nine plus sixteen is twenty-five, and they fill it exactly. So the square on the hypotenuse equals the two other squares added together. In symbols, c squared equals a squared plus b squared, where c is the hypotenuse. It works for every right-angled triangle. Change the sides, and the two totals always match. But bend that corner away from ninety degrees, and they stop matching. No right angle, no Pythagoras. The rule is named after Pythagoras, a Greek mathematician, but people in Babylon and India knew this pattern before him. Back to the throw. The two base paths are eighteen point three metres each, and the throw is the hypotenuse. So c squared is eighteen point three squared plus eighteen point three squared. That's three thirty-four point eight nine, plus the same again, six hundred and sixty-nine point seven eight. That's c squared, not c. To get c, take the square root. On a calculator, type the whole sum first, then press square root, so nothing gets rounded on the way. The square root of six six nine point seven eight is twenty-five point eight eight metres. Check it makes sense. It's more than eighteen point three, and less than thirty-six point six, just as we thought. So to find the hypotenuse, square the two sides, add them, then square root.

scenes.teachingReason: Here's the idea behind the theorem. Take the garden bed triangle from before, with sides of three, four and five metres. Draw a square on each side. The square on the three side holds nine unit squares. The square on the four side holds sixteen. Now slide all of those into the big square on the hypotenuse. Nine plus sixteen is twenty-five, and they fill it exactly. So the square on the hypotenuse equals the two other squares added together. But bend that corner away from ninety degrees, and they stop matching. No right angle, no Pythagoras. The rule is named after Pythagoras, a Greek mathematician, but people in Babylon and India knew this pattern before him.

scenes.teachingReason: Sometimes you know the hypotenuse and need a shorter side. This flying fox platform has a ladder leaning against it. The ladder is three point two metres long, and its foot is one point one metres out from the platform. How high does it reach? Ten point two four minus one point two one is nine point nought three, and its square root is about three point nought metres. Notice we subtracted. If you add instead, you get three point three eight metres, which is longer than the ladder itself. That can't be right. A shorter side always comes out shorter than the hypotenuse.
